analysis.investment_thesis: Kansai Nerolac fails both legs of the Magic Formula: earnings yield of ~5.7% (EBIT ₹942 Cr / EV ~₹16,625 Cr) is below my 6% minimum, and ROCE of 13% is well below my 20% threshold for a "good" business. At 26.6x P/E with only 8.5% revenue CAGR and shrinking operating margins, you're paying a full price for a mediocre-return business — the antithesis of Magic Formula investing.
key_strengths: Near-zero leverage (D/E 0.04) with consistent OCF positive in 5/5 years, providing financial stability.
Strong promoter backing from Kansai Paint Japan (74.96% stake) — a globally reputed coatings major with technology support.
Entrenched industrial/automotive coatings franchise giving some revenue diversification beyond crowded decorative paints.
key_risks: ROIC at ~13% is structurally weak — a paint company losing share to Asian Paints (ROIC ~40%+) and Berger in the high-margin decorative segment.
Operating margins at only 9.07% (EBITDA margin ~11.8%) are compressed; EBITDA CAGR over 9 years is a paltry 4%, showing inability to translate revenue growth into earnings.
Core earnings quality is poor: Other Income of ₹769 Cr (2025) nearly equals operating income of ₹942 Cr — strip that out and the core business earns almost nothing at this market cap.
red_flags: Other Income (₹769 Cr) is ~82% of EBIT (₹942 Cr) — net profit is heavily propped by non-operating income (likely investment gains from parent entity transactions), masking weak core profitability.
FCF is wildly volatile: -₹193 Cr in 2022, ₹545 Cr in 2021, ₹347 Cr in 2025 — signals capex cycle risk and poor earnings predictability.
Revenue has stalled: ₹7,801 Cr (2024) vs ₹7,823 Cr (2025) — essentially zero growth in the latest year while capex rose to ₹326 Cr.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Kansai Nerolac yields a failing grade on both dimensions. Earnings Yield = EBIT ₹942 Cr / EV (₹16,423 Cr mkt cap + ₹296 Cr debt − ₹94 Cr cash = ₹16,625 Cr) = **5.7%** — below my 6% floor, meaning you're not even getting a cheap price for a mediocre business. Return on Capital proxied by ROCE is 13%, far short of my 20% threshold. Compare this to Asian Paints or even Berger, which consistently post ROIC north of 30-40%. Greenblatt's formula only works when both metrics are high; here both are low, which is the worst combination.

The most glaring issue is earnings quality. The ₹769 Cr "Other Income" in FY2025 nearly matches the entire ₹942 Cr operating income — strip it out and core pre-tax profit collapses. Net profit CAGR of just 2.3% over 9 years on 8.5% revenue growth tells the real story: this business is not earning attractive incremental returns on the capital it deploys. With capex rising to ₹326 Cr in FY2025 and FCF falling to only ₹347 Cr, capital intensity is heading in the wrong direction. At 16.9x EV/EBITDA, the market is pricing in a quality business that the fundamentals don't support.
